items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Coleman Hawkins was the star in New York

ctx.x: Oh yeah. When you slap your tongue against the reed, it has a popping sound.

That’s what they used to do. You would do more of that than you done variations. David Jones didn’t come there with no slap tongue. David Jones run the changes all over the place. There were all the saxophones. Coleman Hawkins was the star in New York, because he was doing the [“cluck cluck cluck” sound]. They told him, you

better go up there and hear that cat from New Orleans. That’s how, that’s the greatest scene he created. He went up there and heard David Jones, and he listened and he listened and he listened. He got off a couple of nights from Fletcher’s band to go up there and hear David Jones. Next when David Jones and them left the Savoy, Coleman Hawkins had a new style. But if you say that, people are going to say to you, Lee Collins taught me that. David Jones stop all that slap tonguing. They start running variations,…

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: He was crazy about Hawk. 'Who was the greatest?' And he'd talk about the greatness... He was his idol. He worshipped...idolized...

ctx.x: David Jones, yeah. A fantastic musician. He's the man that when he went to New York with the Missourians... He went to St. Louis, he joined R.Q. Dixon and them in Missouri, and he went to New York. And he was a terrific tenor saxophone player. He played legato. See, Hawk and them people in New York was playing staccato and slap tonguing. That would have been ...(?)... And they heard David Jones, and they all come to play legato.
